No listed comorbidity, weight/BMI value, or age changes the dose of hydrochlorothiazide here, but none of those are what makes the prescription wrong. PHARMACOLOGICAL BASIS
Naproxen is a nonselective NSAID inhibiting COX-1/2 and prostaglandin synthesis. It is hepatically metabolized (CYP2C9/1A2/2C8) with renal excretion. Chronic hypertension adds NSAID-related sodium/water retention and BP elevation. Acetaminophen PRN has no clinically significant interaction; food only reduces GI upset.

PATIENT-SPECIFIC ANALYSIS
At 26 weeks, she is beyond the 20-week threshold for avoiding NSAIDs. Pregnancy therefore changes management: naproxen should be replaced by acetaminophen and nonpharmacologic measures. Chronic hypertension independently argues against NSAIDs because of BP elevation. Normal maternal renal/hepatic function does not offset fetal risk; no dose adjustment is relevant because the issue is agent selection. Sickle cell trait, BMI 22.1, age 30, remote alcohol, no tobacco/substance, seasonal rhinitis, and caffeine intake do not alter this conclusion. No allergy or interacting drug is present.

Respiratory Impairment Risk: FALSE - seasonal rhinitis without asthma/AERD.

Infection Risk: FALSE - no infection.

Tobacco Use Risk: FALSE - never used.

Caffeine Intake Risk: FALSE - high intake but no clinically significant naproxen interaction.
Weight/BMI Risk: FALSE - BMI 22.1 is normal.
Age Risk: FALSE - age 30 is not a risk factor.

Unsafe. Naproxen should not be prescribed in this 26-week pregnant patient with chronic hypertension.
